extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students, and readers learning the logic of scientific inquiry and induction (e.g., philosophers of science, geologists, experimentalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming, testing, and judging scientific hypotheses and empirical (derivative) laws — including when to accept hypotheses, how to infer past causes from present effects, limits of empirical generalization, and how to treat progressive/accumulating effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis acceptance and parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Try hypothesis after hypothesis until one is found which fits the phenomena; which one, when found, is to be assumed as true, with no other reservation than that if on re-examination it should appear to assume more than is needful for explaining the phenomena, the superfluous part of the assumption should be cut off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept hypotheses that fit observed phenomena, but prune any part of the hypothesis that is unnecessary for explanation (Occam-like parsimony). This rule is applied regardless of whether multiple hypotheses might equally fit the data; unnecessary assumptions should be removed upon re-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer known agents and laws in historical inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Endeavouring, in conformity with known laws, to conjecture what former collocations of known agents may have given birth to individual facts still in existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring past events (e.g., geology, judicial reconstruction), prefer explanations invoking known agents and established laws rather than inventing novel agencies or properties. The legitimacy rests on using causes known to produce similar effects in current experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of absence of other known causes (circumstantial proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is enough, for most purposes, if no other known cause could have generated the effects shown to have been produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstantial evidence can justify inference to a past cause when no alternative known cause explains the observed effects (analogy to determining murder from bodily signs). This permits reasonable historical inferences even in absence of direct eyewitness proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing unknown substances or unknown properties
rubrics_metrics.description: There is in [Laplace's theory] no unknown substance introduced on supposition, nor any unknown property or law ascribed to a known substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer theories that do not posit new, unexplained entities or novel laws when known laws and substances suffice to account for the phenomena. Introducing unknowns is a weaker explanatory move and should be avoided unless necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in extrapolating present laws to the remote past or other contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: There would still be a much greater chance of error in assuming that the existing laws of nature are the same which existed at the origin of the solar system, than in merely presuming (with geologists) that those laws have lasted through a few revolutions...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit extensions of laws beyond the range of direct experience (deep past, other planets, different collocations). Recognize increased uncertainty when assuming unchanging laws over vast times or different conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish proximate vs remote causes in successive effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The original projectile force... is the remote cause of all its motion, however long continued, but the proximate cause of no motion except that which took place at the first instant. The motion at any subsequent instant is proximately caused by the motion which took place at the instant preceding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing sequences (e.g., motion), identify the proximate cause at each stage rather than attributing every later effect directly to the original cause. This avoids mistaken causal attributions across successive links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat continuous causes as compositions of successive causes (progressive effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause which continues in action, must on a strict analysis be considered as a number of causes exactly similar, successively introduced, and producing by their combination the sum of the effects which they would severally produce if they acted singly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model sustained causes as many small successive actions whose accumulated effects form the progressive phenomenon; use mathematical tools (differential calculus) where infinitesimal increments are involved to compute results.

rubrics_metrics.name: When causes change progressively, account for unequal and qualitative changes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the cause does not merely continue in action, but undergoes, during the same time, a progressive change in those of its circumstances which contribute to determine the effect... the quantities added are unequal, and even the quality may now be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a continuing cause itself changes (e.g., seasonal solar changes), account for both accumulation and the evolving character of the cause; the effect will reflect both the cumulation and the changing nature of the causal contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for feedback: effects can react on causes and alter future action
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the causes themselves are permanent... the changes which take place in the quantities and relations of the causes are actually caused by the periodical changes in the effects. The causes... having produced a certain motion, that motion, becoming itself a cause, reacts upon the causes, and produces a change in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize mutual interaction where effects feed back to modify the causes (example: planetary motion), producing complex outcomes like periodicity or non-returning paths. Analysis must allow for reactive alteration of causal conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume succession implies direct causation between successive stages
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not on this account presume that any two successive terms of the series are cause and effect. We presume the contrary; we expect to find that the whole series originates either from the continued action of fixed causes, or from causes which go through a corresponding process of continuous change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between simple sequence and causal dependence; successive stages may both be effects of a common underlying cause rather than one producing the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and provisional status of empirical (derivative) laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific inquirers give the name of Empirical Laws to those uniformities which observation or experiment has shown to exist, but on which they hesitate to rely in cases varying much from those which have been actually observed, for want of seeing any reason why such a law should exist. It is implied... that it is not an ultimate law... it is a derivative law, the derivation of which is not yet known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirical laws as observed regularities awaiting explanation; they are provisional and should not be treated as ultimate causal laws until resolved into underlying laws or supported by deductive explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative laws depend on laws plus collocations; collocations are not reducible
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative laws... depend on those ultimate laws, and an ultimate fact; namely, the mode of coexistence of some of the component elements of the universe. This last-mentioned element... cannot itself be reduced to any law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating derivative laws, consider both underlying causal laws and the particular collocation (arrangement/initial facts) of causes; note that collocations may be contingent and not governed by general laws, limiting generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws valid only within observed limits of time, place, and circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws... can only be received as true within the limits of time and place in which they have been found true by observation: and not merely the limits of time and place, but of time, place, and circumstance...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extend empirical generalizations beyond the specific contexts in which they have been observed without further evidence; examples include geological strata rules or terrestrial coal-bed rules that may not hold on other planets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement alone insufficient to establish causation
rubrics_metrics.description: No generalization amounts to more than an empirical law when the only proof on which it rests is that of the Method of Agreement. For it has been seen that by that method alone we never can arrive at causes... The method affords no means of determining which of these uniformities are laws of causation...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concluding causal laws from simple concurrence across cases (Method of Agreement) alone; seek Method of Difference, controlled experiment, or deductive explanation to distinguish true causes from mere correlated uniformities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign that a uniformity is derivative: evidence of an intermediate link
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sign is, if between the antecedent a and the consequent b there be evidence of some intermediate link; some phenomenon of which we can surmise the existence... if there be such a phenomenon (x), it follows that even if a be the cause of b, it is but the remote cause...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an observable intermediate phenomenon is suspected or detected, treat the apparent a→b regularity as likely resolvable into sub-laws (a→x and x→b). Look for intermediary variables or mechanisms as evidence the law is derivative rather than ultimate.
